blocks.text: 9.2.3. Proxy Pattern

The order service wraps its inventory client in a retry proxy: one `InvocationHandler` that tries a call up to three times when it fails with `IOException`. Since the release, the warehouse logs show exactly one call per stock check, even during a network blip. The order code catches `IOException` and shows "unavailable", and it now fails those requests with `java.lang.reflect.UndeclaredThrowableException`, an exception nobody on the team throws.
A proxy implements the same interface as the object it stands for and controls how calls reach it. `java.lang.reflect.Proxy` builds one at run time, with one handler for every call.
One InvocationHandler Receives Every Call on Every Method of the Proxied Interfaces
The hand-written metrics decorator of unit 8.4.3 repeats the same `try`/`finally` in each of its four methods. A dynamic proxy writes it once:
`Inventory` has `int stock(String sku)` and `void reserve(String sku, int qty)`, both declaring `IOException`. `timed` wraps it, and also a `String` seen as a `CharSequence`:

Inventory.stock took 2154 µs
  Inventory.stock took 25 µs
  Inventory.reserve took 3615 µs
  CharSequence.length took 613 µs
  CharSequence.charAt took 714 µs
length 5, first B
class: $Proxy0, instanceof WarehouseInventory: false
proxy of String: java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: java.lang.String is not an interface

`newProxyInstance` generates a class (`$Proxy0`) implementing the listed interfaces. Each of its methods passes `invoke` the proxy, the `Method` and the arguments (`null` when there are none). The handler names no interface, so it works for any, the JDK's included. The first call to each method was slow because `Method.invoke` sets itself up on first use.

The proxy is not a subclass of the target: `type.cast` to the interface succeeds, a cast to `WarehouseInventory` throws `ClassCastException`, and `Proxy` refuses a class outright. Proxying a class takes a subclass generated as bytecode, which is what CGLIB (copied inside Spring) and Byte Buddy's subclassing do, and a final class such as `String` can't have one. Unit 10.3.3 covers `Method` and reflection itself.
equals, hashCode and toString Reach the Handler Too, So the Handler Decides the Proxy's Identity

The timing proxy now wraps a stock listener, `timed = Timing.timed(new ReorderListener(), StockListener.class)`, whose `toString` is `reorder-listener`. It is registered in an `ArrayList`, printed in a log line, and removed when its screen closes:
Once through `Timing`, once through `TimingFixed`, whose handler begins with the `switch` shown further down:

forwards everything:
  StockListener.toString took 277 µs
registered reorder-listener
  StockListener.equals took 905 µs
removed: false, still registered: 1
answers Object's methods:
registered timed reorder-listener
removed: true, still registered: 0

The proxy sends `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString` to `invoke`, with `Object` as the method's declaring class; `getClass` and `Object`'s other methods it doesn't. The first handler forwards them like any call. `remove(timed)` asked the proxy `equals(timed)`, the handler asked the target, and the target, whose `equals` is `Object`'s identity check, said no. The screen is gone and its listener stays registered, receiving every stock change.
The second handler answers the three methods before timing anything:
Identity by reference makes a proxy equal to itself and to nothing else. A handler may choose otherwise, say two proxies over one target being equal, as long as `hashCode` agrees.

The `proxy` argument is the proxy, so whatever the handler does with it comes back through `invoke`. A handler that logs `"calling " + method.getName() + " on " + proxy` calls `toString` on the proxy, which calls the handler again:
printing proxy inside invoke: java.lang.StackOverflowError
<!-- practice 1 -->
Method.invoke Wraps Whatever the Target Throws, So the Handler Must Unwrap It
The retry handler from the opening compiles without a warning. Find why it never retries:

The order code calls `stock` through it and prints the result, or the exception and its cause chain, then how many calls reached the warehouse. `WarehouseInventory(2)` fails its first two calls with `IOException("connection reset")`, and a blank SKU fails with `IllegalArgumentException`:

naive, 2 resets: java.lang.reflect.UndeclaredThrowableException
    caused by java.lang.reflect.InvocationTargetException
    caused by java.io.IOException: connection reset
    calls reaching the warehouse: 1
naive, blank sku: java.lang.reflect.UndeclaredThrowableException
    caused by java.lang.reflect.InvocationTargetException
    caused by java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: blank sku
    calls reaching the warehouse: 1

`Method.invoke` wraps anything the target throws, checked or not, in `InvocationTargetException`. So `e` is never an `IOException`, and the first failure ends the loop. `catch (IOException e)` doesn't compile ("exception IOException is never thrown in body of corresponding try statement"), and `catch (Exception e)` is the quick way to silence the error. The fix unwraps:

retrying after: connection reset
  retrying after: connection reset
unwrapping, 2 resets: stock 42
    calls reaching the warehouse: 3
  retrying after: connection reset
  retrying after: connection reset
unwrapping, 5 resets: unavailable (connection reset)
    calls reaching the warehouse: 3
unwrapping, blank sku: java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: blank sku
    calls reaching the warehouse: 1

Two resets are absorbed. After five, the caller gets the last `IOException`, which `stock` declares, and its own `catch` shows "unavailable". The blank SKU is not retried and arrives as itself. The timing handler of the first section has the same flaw: every exception the warehouse throws through it reaches the caller wrapped twice.
A Checked Exception the Interface Method Doesn't Declare Reaches the Caller as UndeclaredThrowableException

`invoke` is declared `throws Throwable`, so the compiler lets a handler throw anything, and the proxy checks what comes out against the interface method. An unchecked exception, or a checked one the method declares, passes through unchanged. Any other checked exception is wrapped in `UndeclaredThrowableException`, a `RuntimeException`, because a caller compiled against `int stock(String) throws IOException` can't be handed a checked exception it was never told about. The leaked `InvocationTargetException` above was one. The retry library's own checked exception, thrown when it gives up, is another:

if (!(cause instanceof IOException)) throw cause;
if (attempt == ATTEMPTS) throw new RetriesExhaustedException(ATTEMPTS, cause);   // extends Exception

givingUp, 5 resets: java.lang.reflect.UndeclaredThrowableException
    caused by Retry$RetriesExhaustedException: gave up after 3 attempts
    caused by java.io.IOException: connection reset
    calls reaching the warehouse: 3

Every caller's `catch (IOException e)` is skipped, and in a web service the request fails with a server error instead of showing "unavailable". A handler throws the target's own exception, one the called method declares (`method.getExceptionTypes()` lists them), or an unchecked one. A retry library that wants a type of its own, and can't know what each interface declares, makes it a `RuntimeException`.
<!-- practice 2 -->
A Call the Target Makes on this Never Reaches the Proxy

A handler opens a transaction around each method marked `@Tx`, a runtime-retained annotation it finds on the interface method the proxy passes it. Only `place` is marked. A batch method on the same class places several orders:
`orders` is the proxy over an `OrderService`, and the handler prints `BEGIN` and `COMMIT` around each transaction. `orders.placeAll(List.of("O-7", "O-8"))` prints:

placeAll on the proxy:
    placing O-7
    placing O-8

The proxy saw `placeAll`, which isn't marked, and passed it on. Inside the target, `place(id)` means `this.place(id)`, and `this` is the `OrderService`, which knows nothing of the proxy. A proxy intercepts only calls made on the proxy reference. For the same reason, Spring's `@Transactional` on a method called from another method of the same bean is ignored in Spring's default proxy mode.
The fix is to call `place` through the proxy. The loop moves to an object that holds it:

OrderBatch over the proxy:
  BEGIN  place
    placing O-7
  COMMIT place
  BEGIN  place
    placing O-8
  COMMIT place

A default method run with `InvocationHandler.invokeDefault` is different: the target never runs, `this` inside its body is the proxy, and its calls to other interface methods come back through `invoke`.
<!-- practice 3 -->
Summary

items: **One handler receives every call on the proxied interfaces**, for any interface but only interfaces: the proxy is no instance of the target's class, and a class needs a generated subclass.

**`equals`, `hashCode` and `toString` reach the handler.** Forwarding `equals` to a target with identity `equals` makes the proxy unequal to itself, so a list can't remove it; printing `proxy` inside the handler recurses until `StackOverflowError`.
**`Method.invoke` wraps the target's exception in `InvocationTargetException`.** A handler that doesn't unwrap it retries nothing and changes the type of every failure.
**A checked exception the method doesn't declare becomes `UndeclaredThrowableException`**, which skips the caller's `catch`. Throw what the method declares, or something unchecked.
**A call on `this` bypasses the proxy.** Calls that must be intercepted go through the proxy reference, which is why a self-call in Spring ignores the called method's `@Transactional`.

blocks.text: Reference
**What reaches `invoke` (Java 21; `Proxy` and `InvocationHandler` javadoc, and this page's runs):**

rows: `args` is `null` when the method has no parameters
a call the target makes on `this`

blocks.text: **What the caller gets from the handler:**

rows: throws an unchecked exception or an error
throws a checked exception the interface method declares
throws any other checked exception, `InvocationTargetException` included
returns `null` for a primitive return type
returns a value of another type

blocks.text: Challenges

items: The retry proxy wraps an interface whose `reserve` is not idempotent. Which methods should it retry, and how would the handler know? Compare an annotation with a list of method names.
Put the timing proxy and the retry proxy around the same `Inventory`, in both orders. What does the timing line measure in each, and which order do you want on a dashboard?
A listener is wrapped and registered twice by mistake, as two proxies. With identity-based `equals`, can the second registration be detected? Design an `equals` that can, and say what it costs.

blocks.text: Design Note: Why the JDK Proxies Interfaces Only

`Proxy` arrived in Java 1.3. The class it generates extends `java.lang.reflect.Proxy` and implements the interfaces you list. Since it extends `Proxy`, it can't extend your class, and an interface has no state and no constructor, so the proxy only has to answer calls. A subclass-based proxy can't intercept final or private methods, carries the parent's fields unused, and must either run one of the parent's constructors or skip them, which takes a library such as Objenesis.
The JDK can wrap an object only for callers that depend on its interface, the dependency unit 8.1.5 argues for on other grounds. Code that names the class can't be handed the proxy at all.
